name: Assemblage Point
beta: Begin beside a grungy-looking crack on its left, then work up the slab with four bolts.
overview: A short but pleasant slab on a sport route, ending at anchors beside a triangular roof; it also gives access to the Briar Ledge's left part.

current.area_walk_in: Take the Bushwhack Trail off the ridge trail, bearing left where it forks, and keep descending to the wall. The path grows faint; skirt a minor crag with no routes, then go roughly 100 more yards to find the cracks on your left.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.anchor: anchors beside a triangular roof, on its right

name: Vanishing Act
beta: Ascend the conspicuous grey buttress, clipping seven or eight bolts to the anchors.
overview: A bolted line up a conspicuous gray buttress to rappel anchors on a ledge. It was first graded easier, but flaking holds have pushed it into solid 5.12 territory.

current.area_walk_in: Take the Bushwhack Trail off the ridge trail, bearing left where it forks, and keep descending to the wall. The path grows faint; skirt a minor crag with no routes, then go roughly 100 more yards to find the cracks on your left.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.anchor: rap anchors on the ledge above

name: Mae Day
beta: Begin under the roof's right-hand portion at the foot of a large corner, pull out the roof with an undercling (a stick clip helps with the first bolt), then tiptoe up delicate moves ending in a brief crack.
overview: Undercling out of the roof, using a stick clip for the first bolt, then delicate moves lead to a short crack at the top.

current.area_walk_in: The approach trail ends right at the base of Lower Sunset, close to Super Sunset Crack. A short fourth-class scramble just uphill reaches Middle Sunset.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.location: Under the right half of a squat roof, where a big corner (facing right) begins

name: Mosaic
beta: Start atop some blocks beneath a shallow corner that leans leftward, follow it until it finishes, then head upward and rightward to the anchors.
overview: Brief yet excellent. Follow the corner until it ends, then work up and rightward to the anchors.

current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.location: On blocks beneath a shallow corner that leans left (facing left)

name: Oh My God Dihedral
beta:
Climb a short crack of about fifteen feet to a comfortable ledge at the foot of the main corner and belay there.

Then climb the huge corner above; carry every cam size from one to four inches.
overview: Rated among the best routes in the eastern states. A short 5.6 crack leads to a good ledge at the corner's foot, where you belay; the enormous corner (facing left) is the main event.

current.area_walk_in: Take the Bushwhack Trail down off the ridge, keeping left at the fork. The dihedral soon glimmers among trees to the left; step off the path and scramble via a tight gap between boulders to the base.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: Pincer Perfect
beta: Follow Crab Walk's lower portion up to its horizontal crack, then fire up the wall with four bolts; the protection is a mixture of gear and bolts.
overview: A mixed route that shares Crab Walk's opening as far as the sideways crack, then takes the face with four bolts.

current.area_walk_in: Leave the ridge path at the east-facing clearing and slab above God's Area, walk down the slab, and on entering the woods take the left trail downhill along the foot of the slab.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: Praying Mantle
beta: Past the second bolt, keep to the right of the big flake and go directly up the wall, passing a succession of little flakes toward slings threaded through fixed pins.
overview: Departs Scared Seamless once the second bolt is clipped, bypassing the big flake on its right and heading straight over a string of little flakes to end at slings.

current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: Scared Seamless
beta: Ascend the slab beside the ledge's left end, clipping a pair of bolts en route to a flake; stay on the flake, clip one further bolt and set up the belay on slings. A handful of small nuts and cams helps.

current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: Sunset Gun
beta: Muscle up a brief corner leaning leftward, blast across a bulge, and bear right to the anchors.
overview: Muscle up a stubby corner that leans left (facing left), then blast past a bulge and traverse rightward onto the anchors of Priapus Verde.

current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: Super Sunset Crack
beta:
Follow the slender crack slanting leftward to the anchors; technical and strenuous.

Carry a handful of little cams (roughly half an inch to an inch) for the start and the end, as placements are scarce at the crux, where the seam seals shut.
overview: Technical and strenuous: a slim, leftward-slanting crack leads to the anchors, and gear is nearly impossible to place at the point the crack closes up.

current.area_walk_in: The approach trail ends right at the base of Lower Sunset, close to Super Sunset Crack. A short fourth-class scramble just uphill reaches Middle Sunset.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: Thar She Blows!
beta: Boulder through sporty moves from a short corner up to bolt one (a lengthy stick clip, or gear in the neighbouring Crab Walk flake, can help), then continue to a horizontal break, clip three more bolts, and step left to finish across a flake then slab.
overview: A bolted line on the Whale's Lip slab that ends close to Autumn Harvest, topping out via a flake then slab.

current.area_walk_in: Leave the ridge path at the east-facing clearing and slab above God's Area, walk down the slab, and on entering the woods take the left trail downhill along the foot of the slab.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: The Ally
beta: From the right part of the raised ledge on the face's left side, go by a bolt toward a pin set in an angled seam, pass a flake and reach a second bolt, then take the face with two more clips to the top.
overview: A bolt, then a piton set in the slanting seam; after that a flake, another bolt and two more bolts lead to the top.

current.area_walk_in: Descend from the Ridge Trail beside the Whale's Lip wall, quit its descent path after about 50 yards, and bushwhack rightward around a small outcrop. Drop down the vegetated slope for around 100 yards until a corridor between huge blocks appears on your right. Walk through it to the foot of the big slab.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.location: Beside the rightmost portion of a raised shelf running along the face's left half

name: The Eagle's Gift
beta: Begin in a short corner opening rightward, then meander up the face clipping four widely spaced bolts.
overview: Celebrated yet bold. The face is climbed with just four widely spaced bolts.

current.area_walk_in: Descend from the Ridge Trail beside the Whale's Lip wall, quit its descent path after about 50 yards, and bushwhack rightward around a small outcrop. Drop down the vegetated slope for around 100 yards until a corridor between huge blocks appears on your right. Walk through it to the foot of the big slab.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.location: First line beyond the hallway exit, starting from a short corner (facing right)

name: The Latest Trick
beta: Tackle the very thin central stretch of the wall with four bolts to a horizontal break, then clip a fifth bolt and continue to the top.
overview: Called the nicest, best-protected line on the wall. A very thin central stretch on bolts leads to a horizontal, with one more bolt before the top.

current.area_walk_in: Leave the main ridge path at the clearing and slab that face east; where a path forks at the slab's bottom, bear right and keep going directly through the trees. About 75 yards on, a cluster of rock outcrops appears, and the routes sit on one east-facing wall.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: The Streak
beta: Use the good holds beside the streak, then shift left toward anchors above a big ledge.
overview: A gentle-angled slab following a dark water streak at the right end of the wall.

current.area_walk_in: Find a cave-like opening among the huge blocks at the right end of Middle Sunset, hike back through it about 30 ft, and look for a cairn on the left. A short fourth-class scramble from there reaches the Upper Sunset ledges.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.location: On the right side of the upper wall, up a dark water streak on a low-angle face

name: The Unchained!
beta: On the right part of the gentle buttress, tackle a few difficult moves to reach bolt one (or stick-clip it), after which a much easier flake leads to the anchors.
overview: Hard moves lead up to bolt number one (a stick clip is an option); a far easier flake then leads to the anchors.

current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.location: Over toward the right-hand edge of the gentle buttress

name: The Untamed
beta: Climb the centre of the face clipping three bolts, and complete the route via a flake to the anchors; carry a slim rack of tiny wires and cams, mainly for the start and the end.
overview: Plenty of good climbing. Bolts guard the center of the face, and a flake carries you to the anchors above.

current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: Crab Walk
beta: Start as Thar She Blows does but bear right straight away to the evident flake, climb it to the horizontal break, then follow that break far across to the right until slab climbing takes you to the top. Carry a middling rack of mostly smaller protection.
overview: The easiest line on the slab, though not the most direct. A flake leads into a horizontal break, which is followed all the way rightward until the slab above can be climbed to the top.

current.area_walk_in: Leave the ridge path at the east-facing clearing and slab above God's Area, walk down the slab, and on entering the woods take the left trail downhill along the foot of the slab.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.location: shares its start with Thar She Blows, then moves right at once toward the prominent flake

name: Z-slash
beta: Climb the face while roughly tracing the lightning-bolt-shaped crack system, with a vicious move leaving the horizontal.
overview: Follows the zigzag crack system up the face. A superb route, though the move leaving the horizontal crack is fierce.

current.area_walk_in: Follow the canal or river trail to the plaque at the second lock, where the trail turns right into the woods. About 200 yards on it swings back toward the river over worn rocks; past a numbered marker stake sits a broad point of rock, with the climbs below it.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)
current.location: Ten ft along from Armbuster, on its right

name: North Mowich Headwall
beta: Grade IV, WI3 Moderate Snow. Steep hourglass rock/ice section (40-50 ft), ~45° snow slope, 5th class rock band, ~4,000 ft of climbing from the bivy to Liberty Cap. Rockfall hazard (climb early). Crevasses, avalanche debris. Bivouac at 9,600 ft between North Mowich and Edmunds Glaciers. Two-day approach recommended. Best June-August.
overview: A Grade IV ice route on the northwest side climbing directly up the North Mowich Glacier headwall to Liberty Cap, with a short rock band crux partway up.

current.approach: Northwest corner of Mount Rainier National Park, from Mowich Lake; the SR 165 road to the lake has had no public access since the Fairfax Bridge closed permanently in April 2025
approach_variant_names: Mowich Lake and Spray Park to the bivy between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers
current.descent: From Liberty Cap, cross to the main summit area or descend directly via Emmons-Winthrop to Camp Schurman.
current.detailed_rack: Screws, pickets, and a light rock rack for the hourglass entry and rock band.
current.pro_needs: Mixed protection — ice screws for the entry hourglass, pickets on the snow slope, a few rock pieces for the upper band.

name: A Little Something
beta: Short, straightforward climbing to a bolted anchor.
overview: Sport climb on Megadike North.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: pull over at 1.1 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, at the spot on the left (SE side) where a dirt road joins the pavement, or drive on to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.
current.descent: Lower from the anchor (4 bolts to shuts) on a single strand.
current.detailed_rack: 4 bolts to shuts.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted (4 bolts).
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Megadike North (The Dikes, WA). Megadike North walls run up to ~120ft, so a 70m rope is recommended for margin when lowering off anchors.

name: A Servant To Liberty
beta: Follows Freedom or Death for its first three pitches (5.10, 5.11, 5.11), then takes a right-leaning overlap (P4, 5.12-) into a traverse with layback flakes and a mantle (P5, 5.12-), an arete with a big hand-rail traverse (P6, 5.12), a 165 ft 'mega slab' pitch with 14 bolts and 4 crux moves (P7, 5.12+), and a razor-thin slab crux (P8, 5.13-) before easing off through P9-P11 (5.10-5.10+).
overview: Also published as 'A Slave to Liberty' (450m, Grade V, 5.13-). It follows Freedom or Death for its first three pitches (5.10, 5.11, 5.11) before cutting right to join Thin Red Line just below its third-pitch anchor before launching into eight new pitches (four rated 5.12) up the East Face, with the crux 5.13 slab on pitch 8. Mikey Schaefer began equipping the line in 2015 and completed a one-day free ascent, leading every pitch, in early August 2016 with Shanjean Lee's support.

current.approach: Same East Face approach as Freedom or Death and Thin Red Line: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus. This route starts at the Freedom or Death line — locate that start among the East Face cluster of routes rather than the Liberty Crack or Thin Red Line starts.
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, to the Freedom or Death ramp
current.descent: From the top, either scramble to the summit roped and take the standard Liberty Bell descent, or rappel with two ropes down Thin Red Line's line: rappel with two ropes off M&M Ledge (fixed pin/wire anchor), then move climber's-left to bolted anchors for four double-rope rappels back to the base — five rappels total, all on bolted stations after the first.
current.detailed_rack: 2x #0 C3 to #.75, 1x #1 to #3, one set of small to medium nuts, 8 quickdraws, 6 shoulder-length slings, and 2 ropes if rappelling.
current.pro_needs: Heavily bolted on the upper slab/face pitches (P4-8, including a 14-bolt mega-slab pitch); trad gear needed on the shared lower Freedom-or-Death pitches and upper crack pitches.

name: North Ridge
beta: Rather than the popular Scatter Lake approach, this line reaches Abernathy from Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing a spur ridge from a small tarn onto the main north ridge, then scrambling the crest — weaving around or over gendarmes — to the top. Route-finding is loose and 'pick-your-own-adventure' in spots; parties report it as noticeably harder and slower than the standard route.
overview: Abernathy Ridge's highest point is Abernathy Peak, between the Twisp River and Wolf Creek drainages in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. The more heavily traveled standard route climbs from Scatter Lake on the south side (class 2); the North Ridge described here is a quieter, more sustained class 2-3 alternative reached from Wolf Creek and Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing past an old mining camp at a small tarn and up a spur ridge onto the crest before scrambling to the summit.

current.approach: Start at the Wolf Creek Trailhead (about 3,000 ft), reached from Winthrop by Twin Lakes Road, Wolf Creek Road and a gravel Forest Service road to its end. Wolf Creek Trail #527 drops a couple of hundred feet to the creek and then rolls up the valley through forest heavily burned in 2021, entering the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness early on; it is a long, up-and-down walk of about 10 miles to Gardner Meadows at the end of the trail, where most parties camp. From one of the last campsites, a faint path crosses Wolf Creek and continues up the far side toward Abernathy Lake; it is an old, abandoned trail that disappears in the old burn, so the rest is off-trail. Stay high above Abernathy Lake rather than dropping to it, and make a rising traverse into the upper basin with a small tarn, where the remains of an old cabin and mining equipment mark the old mining camp; a stream just below the tarn is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising to the main north ridge, which has a few exposed class 3 moves, then follow a short boot path along the crest past more mining remains. The path fades past the mine, and the rest is class 2-3 scrambling on boulders and scree to the summit. The upper slopes face south and are normally snow-free from about early July; earlier, firm snow can make the loose talus easier at the cost of carrying an axe.
approach_variant_names: Gardner Meadows to the north ridge
current.descent: Abernathy Peak's North Ridge is a scramble, not a technical roped climb, and no fixed rappel anchors exist on this route — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the class 3 ridge crest north back toward the top of the spur ridge (the route's crux terrain, with a couple of noticeably 'intense' exposed spots — face in and downclimb deliberately here, since the same loose, eroded rock that's manageable going up is more consequential coming down). From there, most parties drop down the scree slope toward the tarn with the old mining camp rather than reversing the spur ridge; an old path leaves the crest and descends to the upper lake. From the tarn, retrace the rough off-trail line past Abernathy Lake back to Gardner Meadows and follow the Wolf Creek Trail out to the trailhead. This is a 0-rappel walk-off/downclimb in normal summer conditions — no rope, rack, or anchors needed. Parties who ascended on firm early-season snow should be ready to descend the upper slopes via glissade or a controlled snow descent with an ice axe instead of scree, and should watch for rockfall from parties above given the generally loose rock on this route.
current.detailed_rack: No roped rock rack is carried on this route. The non-standard North Ridge is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble; no rope or rack is used. Parties do not place cams or nuts or use a rope.
current.pro_needs: None placed — this is unprotected scrambling, not protected rock climbing. Hazard is loose rock/footing (talus, scree, old mining debris) rather than lack of gear placements; a helmet is the relevant safety item, not a rack.
current.rope_note: Unroped Class 2-3 scramble on faint paths, talus and a spur ridge to the crest, then along the ridge crest; steep snow or loose rock possible early season, carry an ice axe if snow persists, but no rope or rack needed for the ridge itself.

name: Accendo Lunae (LiB/West Face Var.)
beta: The standard Let It Burn line covers P1-P4 and most of P5; two further pitches (5.12- and 5.11-) then lead into the West Face finish. P1 (5.8): ramp to a thin splitter crack, tree belay. P2 (5.10+): another brief splitter; shift left to a second belay at a tree. P3 (5.12-): a few 5.10 cracks go past a 5.11 slot, where the old fixed pin has been removed and a good cam placement remains; the crux is two bolts while moving left; belay at a two-bolt anchor. P4 (5.11a): a crack in hands and fingers leads to knobs and then a double crack; belay at a bolt and a fixed pin. P5 (5.11+): a flaring crack turns into a lieback; belay on 1" gear at a bench that trends right. P6 (5.12-): a hard flake/crack sequence; belay in the chimney to the right of a razor flake. P7 (5.11-): go up a tips V-slot, reaching a roof, then a corner. P8 (5.11+): hand crack to a roof. P9 (5.10): chimneys that overhang lead to a big ledge. P10 (5.6): 300 feet of easy ground to the summit.
overview: Accendo Lunae (Latin for 'Burning Moon'/'Illuminating Moon') is a West Face variation named partly in homage to Let it Burn and partly because the first ascent finished by moonlight. Established by Blake Herrington, Scott Bennett, and Graham Zimmerman in 2012.

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), take the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain to Colchuck Lake — forest walking along Mountaineer Creek, a log-bridge crossing at 1.5 miles, turning left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, then a final boulder-moraine climb to the outlet (2.5-3 hours). Fill water here. Continue around the lake's west shore to its south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min, exposed to wet-snow slips into July), then break climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Accendo Lunae — a linkup that starts on Let It Burn's line and finishes via a West Face variation — begins at the same point in the base gully as Let It Burn, on the wall's lower-left section, before diverging upward. Expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final scramble to the wall; rope up if uncertain.
current.descent: Because Accendo Lunae finishes by joining a West Face variation, it shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard summit descent: scramble class 3-4 around the right side of the true summit block (bypassing the balanced boulder) to the sandy scree/talus gully, then descend clockwise around the peak back to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr). A short section near the top is sometimes eased with an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn on the east side (natural anchor) rather than downclimbed. No full rappel of the route line itself is needed.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles to 3 inches; gear is reportedly excellent throughout.
current.pro_needs: A standard doubles rack to 3 inches covers the route; fixed pins/bolts protect the two crux 5.12- pitches.

name: Action Potential
beta: From Burgundy Col, the route starts below a clean splitter flake a few minutes below the col. Eight pitches of flakes and cracks of all sizes — including a fun roof-pull/lieback P1, a finger-crack P2, a steep lichen-covered finger-crack crux P3 (5.10c), 4th-class terrain, a fun chimney P5, a poor-rock corner P6, a heads-up, minimal-gear P7 (5.10), and rambling 5.7 terrain to the summit — make for a varied, tough outing that tests route-finding as much as climbing.
overview: Action Potential is a less-traveled 5.10c, Grade III line up Burgundy Spire's East Face (8 pitches, ~800 ft), first climbed by Mark Allen and Mike Layton, July 18–20, 2004. It offers fun, sustained climbing on generally loose, lichen-covered rock: a flake system with a roof pull on P1, a right-trending finger crack on P2, steep finger climbing through lichen on P3, a chimney on P5, and bulgy terrain requiring careful gear on P7, before scrambling to the summit via Burgundy Ledge.

current.approach: Shares the Burgundy Col approach used by Burgundy's other routes. From the SR-20 pullout (~4,310 ft, near milepost 166, ~3.75 mi east of Washington Pass, opposite Silver Star), a boot path drops through talus into forest, passes a register box, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at ~4,080 ft. The trail climbs east (~2,200 ft) to a flat bench/campsite at ~6,460 ft — roughly the halfway point and a common high camp — then works up through loose scree gullies and a final cairned stretch of unstable scree-over-slab to Burgundy Col (~7,770–7,800 ft): about 3 miles and 3,500 ft one-way. Action Potential does not start at the col: from the col, scramble down and around the base of Burgundy's north face (loose rock, sometimes steep snow requiring an axe into midsummer) for about 5–10 minutes until you're below a clean splitter flake — this is the route start, about 15 ft climber's-left of Ultramega OK's twin-crack start, which itself lies beyond the North Face's start. Water is reliable at Early Winters Creek, seasonal near the Bench, and only a trickle near the col; the col's east side sometimes holds snow/ice into summer. The loose scree below the col is the approach's main hazard in both directions.
approach_variant_names: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then 5-10 minutes around the north face to the splitter flake
current.descent: Action Potential tops out in two possible ways, and the descent depends on which finish you take: either climb up past an old bolt to the skyline and ramble class-5.7 terrain to the true summit, or finish by traversing Burgundy Ledge into the standard North Face route. Either way, the descent used by essentially all parties is the North Face's rappel line: with double ropes, plan on 5 rappels from the summit area back down the face — roughly 40m off a heavily slung summit boulder, 55m off bolts to a ledge near a rock arch, 55m off a sling at a constriction to a slung horn, 40m to scree ledges, and a final 60m back to Burgundy Col, 5-10 minutes from Action Potential's own start. Anchors are a mix of slung boulders/horns and fixed bolts; watch for old webbing and be deliberate pulling ropes, since the face has ledges that catch the line. From the base of the last rappel, reverse the Burgundy Col approach to the highway.
current.detailed_rack: Cams in doubles from 0.4 in to #3, a few smaller cams, and a single #4-equivalent; full nut set.
current.pro_needs: Standard double rack in the small-to-mid range covers the crack/flake climbing; the minimal-gear P7 bulges reward careful, patient placements.
bivy: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side

name: South Ridge (via Asa Peak NE Ridge)
beta: Described as the recommended route: gain Asa Peak's Northeast Ridge, traverse to Agnes's south ridge, and climb short technical sections up to 5.6-5.8. From a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass, parties make a rising traverse over snow, talus, and slabs to the south ridge crest south of Point 7760, then rope up and climb Class 4-5 rock over several pitches, on or to the left of the crest. Where the crest gets too craggy, downclimb one pitch to a ledge system and traverse to a whaleback with views of the summit block. From the 7,480-ft south col, traverse a high snowpatch and ascend a broad Class 2-3 ramp just left of a snow-filled gully, dog-legging right to a headwall; a 5.8 chimney (the crux) and one more roped pitch lead to a final ~100-ft Class 2-3 scramble to the summit.
overview: The standard/recommended line on Agnes: gain the south ridge via a high traverse from Icy-Spruce Pass and the Northeast Ridge of Asa Peak, then climb a mix of 4th/low-5th-class ridge pitches and a 5.8 chimney crux on the summit headwall to the top. The peak's first ascent, in 1936, came up from the West Fork of Agnes Creek rather than by this ridge; the second ascent did not follow until 1969, and only fourteen parties had reached the summit by 1987.

current.approach: From High Bridge in Stehekin, follow the PCT/Agnes Creek Trail south roughly 8-10 miles (about 5.2 hours to a Swamp Creek-area camp) to the Agnes Creek/Spruce Creek confluence. Cross Agnes Creek on a log, then Spruce Creek on another log shortly after, and climb steeply northwest off-trail through brush, talus, and slabs to a camp near Upper Blue Basin (~5,000 ft), then continue to a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass (~6,760 ft) for the summit push.
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the last ~100 ft of Class 2-3 terrain, then reverse the roped pitch above the chimney and rappel the 5.8 chimney/headwall (3 rappels total) to regain the upper gully. From there, descend an east-facing snow couloir for roughly 1,400 vertical feet using snow flukes and running belays back to the south col at ~7,480 ft, then reverse the traverse and ridge pitches back toward Icy-Spruce Pass camp. The round trip from high camp takes about 15-16 hours for a typical party and close to 20 for a slow one.
current.detailed_rack: A light rock rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the low-5th-class ridge pitches and the 5.8 chimney, plus a rope, and ideally pickets/flukes for the snow couloir descent.
current.pro_needs: Standard alpine trad rack sufficient for sustained 4th/low-5th class with a short 5.8 crux; snow protection (flukes/pickets) needed for the descent couloir rather than the ascent itself.

name: Ahoot
beta: Bolts lead to a summit anchor; often used as an intro multi-pitch route since it can also be toproped in one long stretch with a 60m rope.
overview: A brief two-pitch line that can also be top-roped with a 60m rope; a friendly first taste of multi-pitch climbing.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. For the Minidike, pull off 1.5 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, on the left (SE) side of the road immediately after the bridge over the river. Cross the road, scramble down the bridge abutment, and follow a trail downstream on the NW side.
current.descent: Two short pitches to a summit anchor; can be lowered on a single strand with a 60m rope from the top, or rappelled in two stages.
current.detailed_rack: Bolted line to a summit anchor; standard sport rack, plus a 60m rope if toproping the full 70 ft in one stretch.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted, two short pitches.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Minidike (The Dikes, WA). Minidike routes are shorter than Megadike; 60m is sufficient.

name: Alice in Wonderland
beta: From the top of Summertime P1, continue up a seam/crack with small gear, then move up and right past a flake with bolts and over a roof (5.11c) to the anchor.
overview: A short continuation pitch that climbs directly out of the top of Summertime's first pitch, following a seam/crack past a flake and finishing over a roof.

current.approach: Summertime Crag uses a different trailhead than the other four areas' shared Blue Lake approach. From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 through Mazama toward Washington Pass (or, coming from Seattle, continue past Washington Pass toward Mazama on SR-20); park at a small pullout on the east side of the highway, just before the larger 'Spires Gully' parking area used to access the Early Winters Spires from the east. From the pullout, descend off the road down through trees, cross Early Winters Creek, follow it briefly downstream, then climb up-slope and contour left to reach the crag — about a 20-25 minute walk with minimal elevation change. The crag stays shaded until mid-afternoon in summer, making it a popular warm-weather alternative when Mazama-area cragging runs hot.
current.descent: Lower or make a single-rope rappel from the top anchor back to the base; reverse the approach to return to the car.
current.detailed_rack: Small gear (small cams/wires) for the seam/crack start, plus a handful of quickdraws for the bolted flake-and-roof finish.
current.pro_needs: Mixed: small trad gear low, then bolts through the crux roof.

name: Round Mountain Trail (Standard Route)
beta: The standard and shortest approach to Alpine Lookout starts at the Round Mountain Trailhead off FR 6910 east of Stevens Pass. Round Mountain Trail #1529 climbs steeply for about the first 1.6 miles through forest and an older burn area, then joins Nason Ridge Trail #1583. The trail undulates along the crest of Nason Ridge, crosses the exposed 'Ninemile Saddle' knife-edge around mile 4.5, and a final 0.3-mile summit spur leads to the staffed fire lookout at 6,237 ft. A longer alternative approaches from the west via Merritt Lake Trail #1588 to Nason Ridge Trail #1583 (about 11.5-12 miles one-way between trailheads, ~4,400 ft gain from that side), used mainly for through-hikes or when the Round Mountain side is inaccessible.
overview: A non-technical ridge-walk trail hike from the east side of Nason Ridge, climbing steadily through recovering burn forest to a saddle, then following the ridge crest to the historic Alpine Lookout at the summit.

current.approach: From Leavenworth, drive US Highway 2 west approximately 17.4-17.7 miles (or from Stevens Pass, drive east about 18 miles) to just past the Nason Creek Rest Area. Turn north (right heading west / left heading east) onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road, Forest Road 6910 -- watch for the turn on a curve with fast highway traffic. Follow FR 6910 (good gravel) for about 4.5 miles, then turn onto spur FR 6910-170 and continue roughly 0.1-0.25 mile to the Round Mountain Trailhead.
approach_variant_names: Round Mountain Trail #1529 to Nason Ridge and the lookout spur
Merritt Lake trail from the west
current.descent: From the lookout, retrace the 0.3-mile summit spur down to Nason Ridge Trail #1583, follow the ridge trail back across Ninemile Saddle, and descend Round Mountain Trail #1529 through the burn area and forest to the Round Mountain Trailhead on FR 6910. No technical descent gear is needed; the main concerns are the exposed knife-edge saddle in poor weather/ice and the sustained steep first/last 1.6 miles.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is used on this route; it is a Class 1 maintained trail hike with no climbing gear required.
bivy: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
Alpine Lookout — day use only, no overnight

name: Rampart Ridge Scramble
beta: From the Rachel Lake / Lila Lake trail junction, an unsigned 'climber's path' marked by a cairn leaves the maintained trail and climbs Alta Mountain's south ridge. The initial section is steep with loose rock and large steps and no shade; the grade then moderates onto a knife-edge ridge with sustained exposure. There are several class 2-3 moves, at least one 6-8 ft near-vertical step with good holds but serious exposure, a class 3 downclimb crux near the top, and multiple false summits before the true summit is reached. The route is non-technical (no rope typically used) but is exposed enough to be unsuitable for anyone uneasy with heights or for dogs.
overview: Alta Mountain is a popular scramble on the long Rampart Ridge above Rachel Lake near Snoqualmie Pass. From the Rachel Lake trail and Rampart Lakes, an enjoyable Class 2 ridge walk and scramble leads along the crest to the summit with excellent views over the Alpine Lakes country.

current.approach: From the Rachel Lake Trailhead (2,800 ft, end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Rd, Exit 62 from I-90), start on Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first ~2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek on gentle grade, crossing several side streams and cascades (reliable water throughout — no need to carry much from the car). At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses Box/Canyon Creek and hits the notorious 'mile from hell': a heavily rooted, rocky boot-beaten climb that gains roughly 1,300 ft in about a mile, with large step-ups and no switchbacks — this is the crux of the approach fitness-wise, not technically hard but brutal with a full pack. The trail tops out at Rachel Lake (4,700 ft, ~3.5-4 mi from the TH); a use trail/climber's path branches right near the outhouse and skirts the north side of the lake, then switchbacks steeply up rocky tread for about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest (~5,100 ft). At the ridge junction, go left (south) for Rampart Lakes or right for Lila Lake/Alta Mountain — for this route, go right toward Lila Lake. The tread is brushy in places but easy to follow; after about 0.3 mile a cairn marks a fork where the Lila Lake trail continues straight and the unsigned climber's path to Alta branches left. Take the left fork, which starts steep and loose with big steps and no shade, and follow the increasingly exposed climber's path along the ridge crest toward Alta's summit block, negotiating three false summits, class 2-3 rock steps, and short sections of real exposure (in one section the path skirts a cliff edge — fall consequences are serious here, and the route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge). A helmet is commonly recommended for the final ridge scramble due to loose rock and exposure. Total one-way distance to the 6,274 ft summit is about 9.5-10 km (matches the 19.3 km round trip) with roughly 3,300 ft of total gain.
approach_variant_names: Rachel Lake, Rampart Ridge, and the cairned Alta turnoff on the Lila Lake trail
current.descent: This is a scramble, not a technical climb — there is no rappelling on this route (rappels: 0). Descend by reversing the exact ascent line: retrace the ridge crest scramble back over the false summits and down the steep, loose lower ridge to the cairned fork, follow the Lila Lake trail back to the Rampart Ridge junction, drop via the steep half-mile rocky switchbacks to Rachel Lake, then retrace Trail #1313 down through the 'mile from hell' (this section is notably harder on tired knees going down — loose rocky step-downs and roots) and out along Box Canyon Creek to the trailhead. Key descent hazards mirror the approach: the exposed ridge-crest sections near the summit (do not descend this route if the ridge is snow-covered or wet — the exposed traverse becomes significantly more dangerous), loose rock on the steep lower ridge (rockfall risk onto anyone below — descend it one at a time), and the steep, rooted, ankle-turning tread on the 'mile from hell' switchbacks. No natural or fixed anchors are used anywhere on this route; parties should not carry a rope expecting to need it, though a short handline could be improvised on the steep lower ridge for less confident scramblers.
current.detailed_rack: No rock rack is used or needed -- this is an unroped Class 2 hands-on-rock scramble, not a roped rock climb. Parties do not carry cams, nuts, hexes, or a rack of any kind on the standard South Ridge/Rampart Ridge route.
current.pro_needs: None -- no technical protection is placed on this route. It is a Class 2 scramble: loose rock and large steps on the initial push, then a narrow, exposed but non-technical ridge crest with several false summits to the true summit. Rock quality on the ridge itself is solid enough for hands-and-feet scrambling; the main hazard is loose talus/scree on the lower approach slope rather than anything requiring gear placement.
current.rope_note: Class 2 scramble along Rampart Ridge from Rachel Lake with one or two easy 2nd-class spots; no rope or rack needed.

name: West Route
beta: From Upper Cathedral Lake, follow a boot path southeast onto the west ridge/basin, then hike scree and grassy slopes northeasterly into a basin around 8,000 ft before a final walk to the summit. Alternatively, from the Cathedral Peak side a gully/col can be used to reach the same upper basin. The route is Class 2 throughout, with brief Class 3 sections depending on line choice; no rope or technical gear is used by most parties. Frequently combined with Cathedral Peak (Class 3, about one mile away) on the same trip. The true (south) summit has one short mantle move onto a block; otherwise it's a walk.
overview: The standard, non-technical line up Amphitheater Mountain: gain the peak's broad west-facing basin (the 'amphitheater') from Cathedral Pass/Upper Cathedral Lake and follow scree, grass, and boulder slopes to the summit plateau.

current.approach: Two common trailheads reach the base: (1) Andrews Creek Trailhead (Trail 504) — from Winthrop, take Hwy 20 to County Road 1213/West Chewuch Road, drive ~6 miles to Forest Road 51, continue ~22 miles to the trailhead at the end of the pavement (3,050 ft). Hike via Andrews Pass and the Boundary Trail to Upper Cathedral Lake (roughly 7 hours for a loaded backpacking pace). (2) Chewuch River Trail/Thirtymile Trailhead — a longer approach (about 20 miles and ~4,900 ft gain to Upper Cathedral Lake), also joining near Cathedral Pass. Most parties backpack in and camp at or near Upper Cathedral Lake (~7,380 ft) before a summit day. From the Chewuch River trail, the Lesamiz Trail climbs to the Boundary Trail just short of Upper Cathedral Lake, a way in used on both a July and a September trip.
approach_variant_names: Upper Cathedral Lake and the west-side boot path
current.descent: From the summit plateau, descend the same scree/grass slopes back into the west basin, then follow the boot path down to the trail and back to Upper Cathedral Lake. Parties combining with Cathedral Peak often traverse between the two via a connecting gully rather than returning all the way to the lake between summits.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard West Route.
current.pro_needs: No trad gear is placed on the standard route - it is a scree/talus/grass walk-up with one short 3rd-class move near the true summit. A rope/harness/rack is only relevant if linking into one of the technical buttress routes (Middle Finger Buttress, Finger of Fatwa, Pilgrimage to Mecca) on the same peak.
bivy: Remmel Lake and the Spanish Camp meadows
Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
current.rope_note: Straightforward Class 2 walk-up from Upper Cathedral Lake via scree/grass slopes to the 8,358 ft summit; no technical gear needed. Distinct from the technical rock routes on the same peak's north wall.

name: Southeast Ridge
beta: Climbs the southeast ridge in about eight pitches up to 5.6 to the southeast spire, a false summit and the lowest of Argonaut's three summits, then carries on to the true summit on the west spire. The lower pitches are blocky and awkward, carry a lot of lichen and are somewhat hard to protect. The line includes two single-rope rappels, or one double-rope rappel, into the notch. The main summit needs a short, non-exposed Class 4 move to its highest block after Class 3 ridge traversing. The Colchuck Col side is the better way to the base; the Ingalls Creek side means a long, strenuous bushwhack.
overview: The Southeast Ridge of Argonaut gives a longer and slightly more technical line to the summit than the northeast ridge, climbing the rocky crest over a series of steps and towers on excellent Stuart Range granite. With sustained moderate climbing, real exposure, and a remote setting, it rewards parties willing to make the long approach into this quieter corner of the range. Route-finding among the towers is part of the challenge and the fun.

current.approach: Start at the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 (roughly 3,650 ft). At about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike/Beverly Creek Trail) — do not miss this junction, as a wrong-fork error onto the Bean Creek Trail is a commonly reported mistake. Continue to roughly 3.1 miles and turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek Trail), climbing to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles (roughly 5,900-6,000 ft), which opens up the first real views of Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail. From the pass, descend the well-maintained trail on the far side to the south shore of Ingalls Creek at about 6 miles (roughly 4,200-4,250 ft); ford the creek (wading or a footlog depending on the season/year) to reach flat camping at the Fourth Creek/Ingalls Creek confluence. From camp, leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb generally north into the gentle, heather-and-slab Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side, working up open basin terrain beside the southeast ridge, the crest that rises from this side to the southeast spire. The roped climbing follows that crest, about eight pitches to the southeast spire. Hazards: the Ingalls Creek ford can be a real obstacle in early season or after rain; the basin approach involves loose talus and, in shoulder season, hard snow that may warrant an axe and crampons; this is a long, remote approach (partial day just to reach the base) so plan for a car-camp or bivy.
approach_variant_names: Beverly Turnpike TH over Fourth Creek Pass to Porcupine Creek basin
Esmeralda over Longs Pass into Ingalls Creek
current.descent: From the true summit, scramble back east along the summit ridge to the top of the South Gully. Its one technical step is a short, blocky rock cleft capped by a chockstone, with a fixed sling above it: rappel it or downclimb it on belay. Below that, descend the long gully and the brushy, forested slope beneath it toward Ingalls Creek, return to camp, and reverse the approach over Fourth Creek Pass to the trailhead. The descent is long, so leave the summit with a comfortable margin of daylight.
current.detailed_rack: Single set of nuts and cams from finger-size through ~3in covers the ridge's crack and corner systems; nothing larger is reported as needed. Bring cordelette or webbing to back up or replace worn rappel slings.
current.pro_needs: Protection is moderate and intermittent on 4th-to-low-5th ridge terrain; parties report finding rappel anchors along the ridge as hoped, implying stations are already equipped and spaced for single-strand rope lengths. A distinct winter/mixed variant (East Ridge to a crossover into the NE Couloir) exists and is far more serious, requiring rock pro placed to protect wind-slab traverses plus ice tools/crampons — that is NOT the standard 5.6 summer rock route and should not be conflated with it.
bivy: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
current.rope_note: A single 60 m rope is standard. The rappels into the notch go as two single-rope rappels, and the chockstone step on the descent gully is short; a second rope only lets you combine the two notch rappels into one.

name: Artic Rose
beta: Well-bolted with good natural gear opportunities. Ideal first route on the crag. South-facing provides good sun exposure.
overview: The easiest route on Half Moon Crag, offering perfect intro to the area with positive holds and excellent protection throughout.

current.approach: Take US-2 east from Seattle/Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway (now Tye Rd), which heads toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite; park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn roughly 1.4 miles from US-2. From there, the on-foot approach follows only faint boot-path traces through open old-growth forest, generally trending uphill and left across a drainage to reach the base of the crag. Expect about 1,000 feet of elevation gain and 45-60 minutes of hiking, with route-finding skills helpful since the tread is intermittent.
current.descent: Rappel directly down the fixed anchors to return to base.
current.detailed_rack: Light sport rack with 8-10 quickdraws, wired stoppers (sizes 1-3), few medium nuts, 60m rope, rappel device, carabiners.
current.pro_needs: Comfortable on 5.6 slab with bolted protection. Good footwork and basic crack skills helpful.
current.rope_note: Trad, single-pitch (~85ft or less); one 60m rope covers the climb and lower/rappel.

name: Astral Projection
beta: Bolted and naturally protected route with good flow. Ideal warm-up climb on the crag. South-facing with reliable protection points.
overview: A slightly easier variant of the other 5.9 routes, featuring juggy slab and positive edges with excellent protection throughout.

current.approach: Take US-2 east from Seattle/Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway (now Tye Rd), which heads toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite; park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn roughly 1.4 miles from US-2. From there, the on-foot approach follows only faint boot-path traces through open old-growth forest, generally trending uphill and left across a drainage to reach the base of the crag. Expect about 1,000 feet of elevation gain and 45-60 minutes of hiking, with route-finding skills helpful since the tread is intermittent.
current.descent: Rappel directly down using fixed anchors at climb exit to return to base.
current.detailed_rack: Sport rack with 10-12 quickdraws, wired stoppers (sizes 1-4), medium nuts (sizes 1-3), 60m dynamic rope, rappel device, locking carabiners.
rack: Cams to ~3in, doubles in finger/hand sizes
current.pro_needs: Comfortable leading 5.9- with mix of bolt and natural gear protection. Good slab footwork and basic crack climbing fundamentals.
current.rope_note: Trad, single-pitch; 60m rope covers the climb and descent.

name: Astroglide
beta: Excellent mix of bolted anchors and natural protection points. Slab features positive holds and consistent climbing angle. South-facing receives good sun exposure.
overview: A classic moderate crack and slab route with excellent gear placements and straightforward climbing.

current.approach: Take US-2 east from Seattle/Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway (now Tye Rd), which heads toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite; park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn roughly 1.4 miles from US-2. From there, the on-foot approach follows only faint boot-path traces through open old-growth forest, generally trending uphill and left across a drainage to reach the base of the crag. Expect about 1,000 feet of elevation gain and 45-60 minutes of hiking, with route-finding skills helpful since the tread is intermittent.
current.descent: Rappel directly down the route using anchors at climb exit.
current.detailed_rack: Medium sport rack: 10-12 quickdraws for bolts, set of wired stoppers (sizes 1-4) for slab cracks, medium nuts (sizes 1-3), 60m dynamic rope, 4-6 locking carabiners.
current.pro_needs: Lead climber comfortable on 5.9 with mix of bolt and natural gear protection. Good slab footwork and crack climbing fundamentals essential.
current.rope_note: Trad, single-pitch; 60m rope covers the climb and descent.

name: Asymptotic
beta: Predominantly bolted with mixed trad protection. Single 60m rope adequate. South-facing provides good sun exposure.
overview: The steepest line on Half Moon Crag, featuring sustained slab climbing with positive holds and consistent gear placements.

current.approach: Take US-2 east from Seattle/Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway (now Tye Rd), which heads toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite; park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn roughly 1.4 miles from US-2. From there, the on-foot approach follows only faint boot-path traces through open old-growth forest, generally trending uphill and left across a drainage to reach the base of the crag. Expect about 1,000 feet of elevation gain and 45-60 minutes of hiking, with route-finding skills helpful since the tread is intermittent.
current.descent: Rap down from the bolted anchors at the top of the climb using a single 60-foot rappel to the base.
current.detailed_rack: Light sport rack with 12+ quickdraws for bolted protection. Bring wired stoppers and medium-sized nuts for occasional slab placements. Single 60m dynamic rope, 4-6 locking carabiners.
rack: Wired stoppers and nuts (optional, for occasional slab placements)
current.pro_needs: Lead climber comfortable on 5.10b slab with bolted protection. Basic trad skills for occasional nut placements helpful but not essential.
current.rope_note: Bolted sport, single-pitch (~85ft or less); quickdraws only, no trad rack needed.

name: Austera Peak
beta: From Eldorado camp, traverse the Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col, go through the col, then follow the north ridge beside the McAllister Glacier to a break at about 7,900 ft, where climbers rappel 75 ft down to the Klawatti Glacier. From there, about 150 ft of 4th and easy 5th class climbing takes you to the sub-summit; a further short pitch (roughly 50 ft of contrived low 5th class climbing on loose rock) on the summit tower reaches the true summit.
overview: A glacier mountaineering traverse to a rugged summit poking out of the Eldorado Icecap, finishing with a short technical scramble/climb up a loose summit tower.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From camp, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) climbing to the high camp on the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier below Eldorado's east ridge. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Important — this route is not on Eldorado Peak itself, despite being filed under the same area: from the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600ft), continue traversing the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti col; Tepeh Towers are passed along this same glacier traverse, and Austera Peak requires further travel across the Klawatti Glacier (including a short rappel from the col) beyond Klawatti Peak — meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado.
approach_variant_names: Eldorado camp, Klawatti Col, and the 75-ft rappel onto the Klawatti Glacier
current.descent: Reverse the route: climb back up the ~75 ft rappel pitch (well-protected 5.5), navigate the moat, retrace the north ridge/McAllister Glacier traverse back through Klawatti Col, and cross the Inspiration Glacier back to camp.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack from 0.3 to 2 inches plus a few long slings covers the summit tower pitch; a 30-60m rope is sufficient given the short technical sections.
current.pro_needs: Minimal — a light rack for the ~150 ft of 4th/low-5th climbing to the sub-summit and the final loose summit tower pitch.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: Southwest Ridge / McAllister Glacier
beta: This is the standard route to Austera Peak, involving glacier travel through some of the most scenic terrain in the North Cascades. From Eldorado Camp, rope up early and traverse multiple glaciers, passing two major cols (one technical) before reaching the summit tower. Most of the route is scrambling and glacier travel with only minimal technical rock climbing.
overview: A remote summit on the high glacier divide near Primus and the head of the McAllister Glacier, Austera Peak is one of the wilder objectives in the Eldorado high country. It is typically reached on multi-day glacier traverses by parties seeking solitude and serious alpine terrain.

current.approach: Drive the Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead (roughly MP 20, ~2,100 ft) — note the flood-related closure near the park boundary that has, in recent years, added a bike or walk-in stretch to reach the actual trailhead. From the parking area, find the log crossing of the Cascade River near the Eldorado Creek confluence; the crossing has been rebuilt repeatedly after flood damage and can be an awkward single-log or jammed-log crossing depending on the year, so scout it before committing. On the far side, pick up the unsigned but well-trodden climbers' path, which pushes through swampy brush and devil's club before settling into open old-growth timber. The path gains roughly 1,500 ft through timber before breaking out onto the first of two wide boulder/talus fields (watch for marmots, and follow cairns/boot track for the path of least resistance through the rock). Above the talus the trail crosses an alpine meadow strewn with rocks and streams — climbers compare it to a smaller Boston Basin — then drops briefly before a slabby rock ramp leads up onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up and crampon here. Parties camp either lower, at Eldorado Creek Basin (~5,600 ft) or Roush Creek Basin (~6,100–6,400 ft), or push on to a high camp near Eldorado's East Ridge/upper Eldorado Glacier (~7,200–7,600 ft) to shorten summit day; trailhead to high camp runs roughly 5–7 miles with about 5,500–6,000 ft of gain, typically 5–6+ hours. From high camp the route to Austera continues as sustained glacier travel rather than a trail: cross the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier (crevasses are worst near Eldorado's east ridge — stay roped and probe), traverse the upper Inspiration Glacier at ~7,800 ft to Klawatti Col, pass Klawatti Peak on its left through the col, and follow Klawatti's north ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier about 0.4 miles to a break in the ridge at ~7,900 ft — the Klawatti–Austera col/notch. This glacier traverse from camp to the base of Austera's southwest side is itself roughly 3 miles with real elevation swings (about 1,280 ft of ascent and 592 ft of descent over 2.8 miles, ~4 hours one-way), crossing three glacier basins and two cols, one of which (the Klawatti–Austera notch) is a technical crux: a moat gap at the col that often requires careful stemming or a short rappel to get down onto the upper Klawatti Glacier before the final traverse to Austera's base. Primary hazards throughout: crevasse fall on all three glaciers (worse as the season progresses and snow bridges soften), a genuinely committing and remote setting with long retreat times, loose rock ('choss') on any exposed rock sections, and route-finding difficulty in flat light or whiteout on the open ice cap.
approach_variant_names: Three glaciers and two cols to the Klawatti-Austera notch, then the chockstone chimney
current.descent: Descent reverses the same glacier traverse and is not a simple walk-off — expect real rappelling on the technical sections. From the summit, the standard line down is the same chimney/chockstone gully used on the ascent (rated roughly 5.2, about 60 ft): parties commonly rappel this in two rappels using anchors already in place at the top of the chockstone gully (slung horns/chockstones — treat as aging, weathered slings and back them up or replace tat as needed; not bolted). Where snow and rock conditions allow, some parties downclimb the class 3–4 line just right of the chimney instead of rapping the full chimney. From the base of the chimney, reverse the broken/exposed 4th-class and low-5th-class terrain back down to the Klawatti–Austera col notch. At that col, accounts describe a further ~75 ft rappel to drop back down onto the Klawatti Glacier where the moat blocks a direct downclimb — old rappel anchors have been found in place there, but on the return leg some parties instead climb back up roughly 75 ft of well-protected 5.5 rather than rappel, depending on which direction they're traveling that day. A single 30–60 m rope is sufficient for both the chimney raps and the ~75 ft (23 m) col rappel; a light rack with a few long slings and a retrievable cordelette/rap tat for backing up old anchors is standard kit. From there, reverse the McAllister/Inspiration Glacier traverse back toward Eldorado high camp — try to complete this stretch while snow bridges are still firm (early morning or on the return leg of a multi-day traverse), since crevasse risk rises sharply on softened afternoon snow. From high camp, reverse the boulder-field and timber descent trail back down to the Eldorado Creek trailhead log crossing. Overall: this is a rappel-and-downclimb descent, not a clean walk-off — realistically 2 rappels off the summit chimney plus a further short (~75 ft) rappel or downclimb at the Klawatti–Austera col, for roughly 2–3 total rappels depending on conditions and which anchors are used that day.
current.detailed_rack: Very light rack: parties recommend roughly 0.3–2in cams (about 4–5 pieces spanning small-to-medium sizes), with no nuts needed — the chockstone chimney (5.2, ~60ft) and the return traverse's 75ft of 5.5 climbing both take small/medium cam placements. Bring a handful of long (120cm) slings to extend over rime/verglas-prone rock and reduce rope drag on the wandering sections, plus a retrievable 6mm cordelette (~18–20ft) to build the rappel anchor at the 7,900ft notch on the Klawatti-Austera col/north ridge of Klawatti.
current.pro_needs: Protection is sparse but sufficient given the short technical sections: the crux chimney and the 75ft of 5.5 on the return are described as 'well-protected' by real parties, but rock is loose in places (typical North Cascades choss) so test placements. The final ~150ft of 4th/low-5th class scrambling to the true summit is commonly soloed or simul-climbed with minimal gear placed — don't expect to protect every move.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
current.rope_note: The published route description explicitly calls for a '30-60M rope' with a light rack — not a double-rope setup. There is one rappel of ~75ft (about 23m) down to the Klawatti Glacier from the ridge notch, well within single-strand range on a 60m rope; a 70m works too if carried for other reasons. Nothing published supports carrying half or twin ropes on this route; a single 60 m rope is the right choice.

name: Bachelor Party
beta: Vertical (crux) start with great bolt placement, transitioning into a slabby upper section.
overview: Harder sport climb on Megadike North.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: pull over at 1.1 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, at the spot on the left (SE side) where a dirt road joins the pavement, or drive on to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.
current.descent: Lower from the anchor (9 bolts) on a single strand; shares an anchor with the adjacent Face Farce.
current.detailed_rack: 9 bolts to the anchor.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted (9 bolts).
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Megadike North (The Dikes, WA). 70m recommended given Megadike North's walls up to ~120ft.

name: Diobsud Creek Glacier
beta: This is a committing multi-day alpine objective requiring glacier travel, crevasse rescue skills, and strong route-finding ability. The route is accessed via heavily forested terrain with significant deadfall obstacles, followed by steep snow and glacier travel to a 6,250 ft saddle camp. The final summit push is relatively short from camp but requires careful navigation in potentially whiteout conditions. Expect to negotiate around cliff bands, navigate through avalanche terrain, and manage steep gully sections.
overview: Bacon Peak carries a small icecap divided into three named glaciers — Diobsud Creek (SE), Green Lake (NE), and Noisy Creek (NW) — high above the Baker Lake / Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness country. The standard climb approaches via the Anderson & Watson Lakes Trailhead (or a shorter, brushier route from Bacon Creek Road), climbs a steep gully to the Diobsud Creek Glacier, ropes up for the icecap, and finishes with a short Class 2-3 scramble to the rocky summit.

current.approach: Drive Baker Lake Road (FR-11) to FR-1106, then FR-1107 to its end at the Watson Lakes Trailhead (~4,360 ft, Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness boundary nearby). Start on the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail (Trail #611), which climbs gently through forest for about 1 mile to a junction with the Anderson Butte Trail (#611.1); stay left/straight on #611. Continue about another half mile to a second junction, about 1.5 miles from the trailhead — the right fork drops 0.5 mile to Lower Anderson Lake, while the climber's route bears left and climbs to a ridge saddle (~600 ft above the trailhead) where the trail crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness before dropping toward the Watson Lakes. From this saddle, leave the maintained tread and pick up a boot path heading south along the ridge, staying high above Lower Anderson Lake, through meadows to Upper Anderson Lake (~5,100-5,300 ft) — the last easy, reliable water before things get rougher. From Upper Anderson Lake, angle northeast up a short wooded gully, then continue across open rock slabs, scree, and lingering snowfields on Mt. Watson's north side, crossing another saddle near 5,300 ft before descending through heather to the Diobsud Lakes basin (figure roughly 5-6 hours car-to-lakes for a fit party) — the last dependable camp/water source below the peak. From Diobsud Lakes the route turns unpleasant: sidehilling across slippery vegetation, brush and cedar thickets, mossy slab scrambling, and steep dirt/scree gullies with real loose-rock hazard lead up onto Bacon's south ridge. Once on the south ridge, broad snow slopes lead onto the toe of the Diobsud Creek Glacier. Rope up here — the glacier holds real crevasse hazard (parties report needing to probe, especially early and late season, though the upper apron is sometimes reported clean in a good snow year) — and climb/traverse northwest toward the col below the summit pyramid (roughly 6,200-6,300 ft), finishing on broad summit snow slopes to a short summit arête. Snow condition (firm morning snow vs. slushy afternoon) matters a lot on both the gully and glacier sections, so an early start is standard. The gully leading from Diobsud Lakes basin up to the south ridge/glacier access can be avalanche-prone in snow-covered conditions.
approach_variant_names: Anderson Lakes and the saddle chain to the northeast camp
current.descent: The standard descent reverses the ascent line: down the summit snow slopes and col, back onto and down the Diobsud Creek Glacier (roped, same crevasse caution as the approach), down through the steep loose gully/south-ridge terrain to Diobsud Lakes, then back over the Mt. Watson sidehill, saddle, and Anderson Lakes ridge path to the Watson Lakes Trailhead. This is a walk-off/glacier-descent — no rappels are used on the standard round trip; the technical difficulty is glacier travel and loose, steep downclimbing rather than anything requiring rope-anchored lowering. Parties continuing north as part of a longer Bacon-Hagan-Blum (or Watson-Bacon-Hagan-Blum) traverse instead descend from the summit down quick snow slopes to the "Bacon Tarns" (small meltwater ponds sitting on a rock bench beneath the Green Lake Glacier), then follow heather and meadow along Bacon's north ridge, passing high above Green Lake toward Hidden Lake, continuing the traverse rather than returning to the Watson Lakes trailhead. Either way, expect the same loose-rock and brush hazards on the south-ridge gully in reverse, and re-assess glacier conditions/crevasse bridges on the return trip since afternoon snow softening changes the picture from the morning ascent.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed — this is a Class 2-3 snow/glacier mountaineering route, not a roped rock climb. No party is known to use cams, nuts, or pitons. Parties describe dirt/scree gullies with loose rock on the lower south approach and open, generally low-angle glacier/snow slopes above — none describe placing rock protection. Carry a thin glacier-travel rope (roughly 30m per 2-3 person rope team), with a few locking biners and slings, for the Diobsud Creek Glacier and Green Lake Glacier crossings.
current.pro_needs: No fixed rock protection is needed or used on this route — it is snow/glacier travel with a brushy/loose-rock approach gully, not technical rock climbing. Crevasse hazard on the Diobsud Creek and Green Lake Glaciers is real but variable by season: parties describe crossing unroped when the glacier is well filled-in with no visible cracks (one party found no visible crevasses but probed for them as a precaution, and a party on a nearby route mentions crossing a moat), while a party on a slightly later-season visit found crevasses beginning to open up and hidden snow bridges, prompting the party to parallel crevasse lines carefully. A thin glacier rope and basic crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks or a Tibloc-style device) is the prudent standard setup rather than a rock rack; The Mountaineers' guided trips to this peak also require crevasse-rescue proficiency and standard glacier gear.
bivy: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
current.rope_note: No rappelling occurs on this route — descent reverses the ascent on foot down the Diobsud Creek Glacier snow slopes, not rope-assisted rappels, so there is no basis for a double-rope rappel setup. A single lightweight glacier-travel rope (~30m, often carried in coils between 2-3 climbers) is the standard tool here, used for glacier-crossing security and potential crevasse rescue, not for climbing pitches or raps. Experienced parties are reported crossing unroped in low-crevasse-hazard (well snow-filled) conditions, but carrying the rope + crevasse-rescue kit is the safe default given open crevasses and a moat found in other seasons.
